chapter_title: NITYĀRCANĀ IN A VIṢṆU TEMPLE (PĀÑCARĀTRA MODE OF WORSHIP)

sections.content:
This section details the initial steps the priest must take before commencing the main worship. (i) The priest performs his personal daily rituals, then comes to the temple, washes his feet and hands, and sips water ceremonially (ācamana) outside the entrance tower. He then prostrates before the main bali-pīṭha and circumambulates the shrine twice. (ii) Upon reaching the sanctum, he performs śaḍaṅga-nyāsa (six-fold placement of mantras on the body) to purify and divinize himself. The six mantras and their corresponding body parts are listed:
ॐ ज्ञानाय नमः। (हृदये)
ॐ बलाय स्वाहा (शिरसि )
ॐ वीर्याय वषट्। (शिखायां)
ॐ ऐश्वर्याय हुं (बाह्वोः)
ॐ तेजसे वौषट् (नेत्रायोः)
ॐ शवत्यै फट् (अस्त्र, शिरसः परितः)
A verse summarizing this is also provided: (ज्ञानं बलं तथा वीर्यमैश्वर्यं तेजसा सह। शिक्तिरेते चतुर्थ्यन्ता नमः स्वाहावषट्तथा ।।). Quotations from the Pādmā-saṃhitā are included to elaborate on the application and significance of these mantras. (iii) The priest claps his hands three times in a specific sequence, as described in a verse from the Vihagendra-saṃhitā. (iv) He stands before the shrine, rings the bell, and opens the doors with the mantra 'om yam vāyave namaḥ', entering with his right foot first. (v) He bows to the main deity, touching its feet in a specific manner while reciting the mantra: जितं ते पुण्डरीकाक्ष नमस्ते विश्वभावन। नमस्तेस्तु हृषीकेश महापुरुषपूर्वज ॥. (vi) After obtaining the deity's mental permission (mānasīm ājñām), he trims the lamps and formally wakes the deity with a series of verses. (vii) He removes the previous day's flower garlands (nirmālya) and places them on the icon of Viṣvaksena. (viii) He then performs the pañca-śuddhi (five purifications): sthāna-śuddhi (place), pātra-śuddhi (vessels), bimba-śodhana (icon), ātma-śuddhi (self), and mantra-śuddhi (mantras), with supporting verses from Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā and Aniruddha-saṃhitā. (ix) The process of cleaning the icon (bimba-śodhana) is detailed, emphasizing the use of soft materials like cloth or grass and forbidding sharp instruments. Verses from Ananta-saṃhitā, Śrī-Praśna-saṃhitā, and Sāttvata-saṃhitā are cited. The priest cleans the main icon and sanctum, while attendants clean the outer areas. A mantra to be recited during cleaning is provided: शुचीह वो हव्या मरुतः शुचीनाग् शुचिग् हि नोम्यध्वरम् शुचिभ्यः। ऋतेन सत्यमृतमाप आयन् शुचि जन्मानः शुचयः सन्तु पावकाः ॥.
sections.summary: This section covers the essential preliminary rituals for the priest, including self-purification, entering the temple and sanctum, performing nyāsa to divinize the body, waking the deity, and conducting the five-fold purification (pañca-śuddhi) of the self, place, vessels, icon, and mantras.

sections.content: This section describes the worship of deities surrounding the main deity. It distinguishes between attendant-deities (parivāra-devatā), who receive daily worship, and enclosure-deities (āvaraṇa-devatā). The worship is necessary to gain permission to approach the main deity. The procedure includes worship of deities at various locations: (i) On the right and left sides of the sanctum (Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa). (ii) On the lintel above the doorway (Śānti, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Rati). (iii) On the doorway itself, including panels, frame, bolt, and key-hole (Viśvanetra, Viśvavaktra, Vedas, Śāstras, etc.). (iv) In the porch in front of the sanctum, including Śaṅkha, Cakra, Tārkṣya (Garuḍa), and deities on the vimāna superstructure. (v) This is followed by the adoration of deities in the five enclosures. The first enclosure (antarmaṇḍala) includes Jaya, Candra, Vijaya, Āditya, Manmatha, Durgā, Viṣvaksena, sapta-mātṛkās, and dikpālas. The second enclosure (antarhāra) includes bearers of Viṣṇu's weapons and the weapons themselves. Worship continues for the other three enclosures. These deities are to be worshipped at three junctures (dawn, noon, eventide) and involves prostrations, water-offerings, garlands, and incense. The section concludes with a description from the Pādmā-saṃhitā of visualizing the entire temple structure as a human body.
sections.summary: This section outlines the systematic worship of attendant and enclosure deities (Parivārārcanā) located on the sanctum doorway, in the porch, and across the five concentric enclosures of the temple, a prerequisite for worshipping the main deity. It also introduces the concept of visualizing the temple as a cosmic body.
key_concepts: Visualization of temple as a body

sections.section_title: Transformation of Body and Self to Acquire Eligibility to Worship
sections.content: This section focuses on the internal transformation of the priest. (i) The priest, properly attired and wearing a pavitra-ring, sits in a specific posture. (ii) He performs 'dig-bandhana' (sealing the directions) using the astra-mantra for protection. (iii) He then undertakes 'bhūta-śuddhi' (purification of the five elements: earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa) that constitute the body. This is a contemplative process involving visualization of seed syllables (yam, ram, lam, vam) to dry up, burn away, and purify the sinful body, ultimately reconstituting it as a divine form. (iv) The ideology behind this is explained: the elements correspond to different parts of the body. The soul (jīva) is visualized as progressively merging the gross elements into the subtle ones, then ascending through the suṣumnā channel to merge with Vāsudeva. The physical body is thus transformed into an immortal instrument fit for worship. (v) The palms and fingers are purified with the astra-mantra. Three types of nyāsa are described—sṛṣṭi, sthiti, and saṃhāra—each suited for different types of worshippers (celibates, householders, those seeking emancipation) and deity postures. (vi) The core of this section is mantra-nyāsa, the placement of mantras on the body to achieve 'tādātmya' (identity) with the deity, based on the principle 'nādevo devam arcayet' (one who is not a god cannot worship God). The priest imagines himself as Vāsudeva. The procedure involves placing mantras for the six divine qualities (ṣaḍ-guṇa) and weapons, followed by the placement of the syllables of the twelve-lettered Vāsudeva mantra (om namo bhagavate vāsudevāya) on various parts of the body.
sections.summary: This section details the crucial inner rituals performed by the priest to become worthy of worship. It covers the purification of the elemental body (bhūta-śuddhi), the transformation of the physical self into a divine instrument through breath control and visualization, and the methodical placement of mantras (mantra-nyāsa) to achieve identity with the deity Vāsudeva.

sections.content: This section transitions from internal preparation to external worship, beginning with mental worship (mānasa-yāga). (vi) Mānasa-yāga is described as a contemplative session where the priest internalizes the entire worship process. He withdraws his senses, focuses his mind, and visualizes a cosmic seat for the deity, built upon layers of supporting energies (ādhāra-śakti), kūrma (tortoise), Ananta (serpent), an ocean of milk, and a divine lotus. On this lotus, aspects of Godhead (Dharma, Jñāna, etc.) and the Vedas are imagined. Within this, the primeval sound (nāda) gives rise to the Vāsudeva mantra. A celestial stream (Gaṅgā) is visualized to provide water for mental offerings (arghya, pādya, etc.). The priest then mentally performs mantra-nyāsa on the visualized Godhead, offers mental worship, performs japa, and concludes with a mental fire oblation (mānasa-homa). The text explains that while mental worship is potent, external worship (bahir-yāga) is necessary to uproot deep-seated karmic traces (vāsanā). (i) The priest then arranges the physical articles and vessels for worship. (ii) He prepares the Yoga-pīṭha (seat of worship) by worshipping its constituent deities (Ādhāra-śakti, Ananta, Dharma, Jñāna, etc.) culminating in a collective worship of the seat itself. (iii) He performs mantra-nyāsa again and then fills the invocation vessel (āvāhana-pātra). Reciting the Vāsudeva mantra, he invokes the deity's presence into the water and then sprinkles it on the icon, materializing the Godhead in it. He welcomes the deity with verses and prostrates. (iv) After providing a seat (āsana), he offers Arghya, pādya, and ācamana with specific mantras.
sections.summary: This section covers the pivotal transition from internal to external worship. It begins with an elaborate description of 'mānasa-yāga' or mental worship, where the entire ritual is performed in the priest's mind. This is followed by the first sequence of formal, external worship ('bahir-yāga'), which includes preparing the ritual seat (Yoga-pīṭha), formally invoking (āvāhana) the deity into the icon, and offering the initial services of welcome.

sections.content: This section details the ceremonial bathing of the deity. First, attendant deities are worshipped on the twelve petals of the seat-lotus (yogasana). (i) The priest requests the deity to move from the main seat to the one prepared for the bath (snānāsana). The text then explains the temple practice of using multiple moveable metallic icons (jaṅgama-bera) for different services, as the main icon (dhruva-bimba or mūla-bera) is immoveable. These include the karmārcā (for general worship), snapana-bera (for bathing), utsava-bera (for processions), etc. At the start of a service, the energy (śakti) from the main icon is ritually drawn into the specific moveable icon. The distribution of power is hierarchical: the karmārcā receives 1/6th of the mūla-bera's power, the utsava-bera receives 5/6ths of the karmārcā's power, and so on. After the bath, the power from the snapana-bera is returned to the main icon. The bath itself is administered to the snapana-bera in the porch (agra-maṇṭapa). Various aspects of the Deity are invoked into the ceremonial vessels (kalaśa) containing different substances (ghee, curds, milk, honey, etc.). The bath is administered methodically with these articles, often to the recitation of the Puruṣa-sūkta. It is performed as if for a living person, including symbolic tooth-cleaning, tongue-scraping, and oiling. A shower-bath through a plate with a thousand holes (sahasra-dhārā) may also be given. Finally, the icon is wiped dry and offered new garments, and a light (ghaṭa-dīpa) is waved.
sections.summary: This section describes the ritual bath (Snāna) of the deity. It introduces the crucial concept of multiple moveable icons (jaṅgama-bera), explaining how divine energy is transferred from the main immoveable icon to a specific one for the bath (snapana-bera). The bathing ceremony is elaborate, involving various consecrated substances and performed as a service to a royal, living person.

sections.content: (i) After the bath, the snapana-bera is returned to the sanctum and its power is restored to the mūla-bimba (main icon). The main icon is then elaborately decorated from crown to toe-ring (kirīṭādi-nūpurāntam). This sequence is figuratively called 'alaṅkārāsana' (seat of decoration), though a special seat is not always used. The priest offers ācamanīya and requests the deity to accept the decoration. He then adorns the icon with ornaments, flower-garlands, and garments. (ii) Collyrium is applied to the eyes with a golden stylus while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. Flowers, sandal-paste, incense, and lights are offered, culminating in a final waving of light (nīrājana). (iii) The ritual of 'mātrā-dāna' (gifting of ration to the priest) is often included here. It involves formally giving rice, sesamum, money, fruits, etc., to the chief priest after showing them to the deity. (iv) The texts prescribe that this sequence should be followed by entertainment for the deity, including dance, vocal and instrumental music, eulogies, and readings from scriptures. Another waving of light concludes the sequence.
sections.summary: This section covers the 'Alaṅkārāsana', the elaborate decoration of the main deity after its ritual bath. It involves adorning the icon with garments, ornaments, and garlands, offering incense and lights, and includes the custom of 'mātrā-dāna' (gifting rations to the priest). The service concludes with entertainment for the deity.

sections.content: (i) This sequence involves offering food to the deity. The priest recites a prayer inviting the eternally-satiated deity to accept the offerings for the sake of the devotee's spiritual fulfillment. (ii) Reciting the bhoga-dāna-mantra, the priest offers preliminary items like arghya, pādya, ācamana, madhuparka, and tāmbūla. Attendants then bring various kinds of cooked food in a procession from the temple kitchen and place it before the icon. The food is consecrated by sprinkling water and presented to the deity with a detailed procedure involving specific mudrās and mantras, visualizing the deity partaking of the meal. (iii) Havis (oblations in fire) is also offered during this sequence, with Pārameśvara-saṃhitā being quoted on the types and measures of offerings. (iv) The food offering is followed by a session of japa (contemplative repetition of mantras). The text discusses the choice of mantra (eight-syllabled for emancipation, twelve-syllabled for prosperity) and the appropriate times for recitation. The priest makes a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and performs Ṛṣyādi-nyāsa and Śaḍaṅga-nyāsa. He then contemplates (dhyāna) on the detailed form of the deity seated in his heart-lotus. Finally, he performs japa using a rosary (akṣa-mālā) or by counting on his fingers.
sections.summary: This section details the 'Bhojyāsana', the offering of food to the deity. It describes the formal presentation of various cooked foods (naivedya), oblations into fire (havis), and the subsequent session of mantra repetition (japa), which is preceded by its own set of preparatory nyāsas and deep contemplation (dhyāna) on the form of the deity.

sections.content: (i) Also known as nityotsava (daily festival), this ritual involves taking the icon designated for this purpose (bali-bera) out in a procession. The icon is accompanied by a vessel of cooked rice, flowers, and water. Food offerings (bali) are made to the attendant deities (Viṣṇu-pārśada) in all the temple enclosures, especially the door guardians and Garuḍa, in the presence of the bali-bera. The remainder of the food is placed on the main bali-pīṭha at the front of the shrine with the mantra 'ओं विष्णुपार्षदेभ्यो नमः'. After the offering, the party circumambulates the bali-pīṭha and returns to the sanctum. The bali-bera is taken inside, and its power is formally returned to the main deity (mūla-bera). (ii) Once this sequence is complete, the doors of the sanctum are closed, signifying the end of the day's main pūjā. The priests circumambulate the shrine and return home. A verse from Pādmā-saṃhitā is quoted, classifying worship ending with bali-utsava as the best type.
sections.summary: This section describes the 'Bali-yātrā' or 'nityotsava', the daily ritual procession where food offerings (bali) are made to all the attendant deities throughout the temple precincts. This is done using a specific moveable icon (bali-bera), and the ceremony concludes with an offering at the main offering stone (bali-pīṭha) before the icon's power is returned to the main shrine.

sections.content: This is the final sequence of worship, performed at night. The deity is formally put to bed to rest in yoga-nidrā (yogic sleep). The priest offers flowers to the main icon and makes a request: स्वामिन् लक्ष्मीश भगवन् सर्वज्ञ पुरुषोत्तम। शय्यासनं मया क्लृप्तं योगनिद्रमुपाश्रय ॥. The icon meant for this service (śayana-bera) is formally worshipped, invoking power from the main icon. The śayana-bera, along with its consorts, is then taken to a special apartment where a bed has been prepared. After the icon is placed on the bed, offerings of Arghya, pādya, ācamana, sandal paste, flowers, and tāmbūla are made. The priest prostrates, asking for forgiveness for any errors in the worship: सर्वं न्यूनातिरिक्तं च मया पूर्वं हि यत्कृतम्। तत्सर्वं देवदेवेश क्षन्तुमर्हसि मे प्रभो ॥. He offers a final handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), attends to the permanent lamp (nitya-dīpa) in the apartment, and closes the door, sealing it with the kavaca-mantra. He requests Cakra and Garuḍa to guard the doors, circumambulates the shrine, and goes home.
sections.summary: This section describes the 'Śayyāsana', the last ritual of the day, where the deity is formally put to rest for the night. A special icon (śayana-bera) is taken to a bed chamber, offered final services, and the priest concludes the day's worship by asking for forgiveness, sealing the chamber, and arranging for its protection.

sections.content: This extensive appendix provides original Sanskrit verses from the Sāttvata-Saṃhitā, which serve as the source material for many of the procedures described in the chapter. The excerpts are organized under topical headings (added by the book's author) that correspond to the stages of nityārcanā. These include: (भद्रपीठशोधनं) cleaning the pedestal; (चक्रराजार्चनम्) worship of the Sudarśana Cakra; (पात्रपरिकल्पनम्) preparation of vessels; (आवाहनम्) invocation; (उपचारसमर्पणम्) offering of services; (स्नानासनम्) the bathing ritual; (भद्रासनशोधनम्) cleaning the main seat; (अलंकारासनम्) the decoration ritual; (भोज्यासनम्) the food offering ritual; (वाह्निसन्तर्पणम्) the fire oblation (homa) ritual in great detail, covering the construction of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), arrangement of implements, purification of ghee, and the different types of oblations; (अनुयागविधिः) the post-offering ritual, including feeding of brāhmaṇas and personal partaking of food; and a detailed description of the yogic practices of the priest after the day's worship, including nyāsa in the reverse order (saṃhāra) and meditation (dhyāna) to achieve union with the divine. The appendix concludes with a note that the text was printed with the commentary of Alasiṅga-bhaṭṭa by Sampurnananda Sanskrit University, Vārāṇasī, in 1982, and the excerpt is from the sixth chapter.
sections.summary: This appendix contains a large collection of Sanskrit verses from the Sāttvata-Saṃhitā, one of the foundational texts of Pāñcarātra. It provides the scriptural basis and detailed procedural instructions for nearly every aspect of the daily worship (Nityārcanā) discussed in the main body of the chapter, from cleaning the altar to the intricate details of the fire sacrifice (homa) and the priest's own spiritual practices.

chapter_summary: Chapter IV, 'Nityārcanā in a Viṣṇu Temple', provides a comprehensive and systematic description of the daily worship ritual according to the Pāñcarātra Āgama tradition. The chapter meticulously details each stage of the worship, beginning with the priest's own preparatory purification rites and entry into the temple. It proceeds through the worship of attendant deities (Parivārārcanā), the crucial internal transformation of the priest into a divine being fit for worship (Bhūta-śuddhi and Mantra-nyāsa), and the performance of mental worship (Mānasa-yāga). The text then describes the main external worship sequences: the ceremonial bath (Snāna) involving multiple moveable icons, the elaborate decoration (Alaṅkārāsana), food offerings (Bhojyāsana), and fire oblations (Homa). The daily ritual culminates with the Bali-yātrā, where offerings are made to all attendant spirits, and the Śayyāsana, where the deity is formally put to rest for the night. The chapter is heavily supported by quotations from various Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās and concludes with an extensive appendix of source verses from the Sāttvata-Saṃhitā, illustrating the scriptural foundation of these practices.
key_arguments: The necessity of the worshipper's transformation: A central tenet is that one must become divine to worship the divine ('nādevo devam arcayet'). This is achieved through rigorous internal purification rites like bhūta-śuddhi and mantra-nyāsa.

Integration of internal and external worship: The chapter emphasizes the relationship between mental worship (mānasa-yāga) and physical, external worship (bahir-yāga), presenting the former as a potent practice and the latter as necessary for purifying deep-seated karmic impressions (vāsanās).

Systematic and hierarchical structure of worship: The rituals follow a strict, logical progression from purifying the space and the self, to invoking and serving the deity in a manner befitting a divine king, encompassing all aspects from bathing and dressing to feeding and entertainment.

The functional use of multiple icons: The text explains the practical and theological reasons for using various moveable icons (jaṅgama-bera) for different services, with a system for transferring the divine energy from the immoveable main icon (mūla-bera).
key_takeaways: Pāñcarātra worship is an extremely detailed, structured, and symbolic process that integrates theology, ritual, and yogic practice.
The priest's role is not merely that of a functionary but of a participant who must undergo spiritual transformation to perform the worship correctly.
The deity is treated as a living, royal presence, receiving a full range of services (upacāras) throughout the day.
The temple is a complex spiritual landscape with a hierarchy of deities, each of whom must be acknowledged and worshipped in their proper place and sequence.
The practices described have a deep scriptural basis, as evidenced by the numerous citations from foundational Saṃhitā texts.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Om, salutations to the Lord Vāsudeva.
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The twelve-syllabled mantra, central to the worship.

quotations.context: Cited on page 15 to explain the purpose of mantra-nyāsa: 'no one who is not a god can worship God', hence the priest must first transform himself into a divine being.

quotations.quote: जितं ते पुण्डरीकाक्ष नमस्ते विश्वभावन। नमस्तेस्तु हृषीकेश महापुरुषपूर्वज ॥
quotations.context: The mantra recited on page 3 by the priest when first bowing to the main deity after entering the sanctum.

quotations.quote: पूजाकाले पुरा कुर्यात् पञ्चशुद्धिं गुरूत्तमः । स्थानशुद्धिं पात्रशुद्धिं बिम्बशोधनमेव च। आत्मनो भूतशुद्धिं च मन्त्रवर्णास्ततो रमे।॥
quotations.context: A verse quoted on page 4 that lists the five purifications (pañca-śuddhi) to be performed before worship.

quotations.quote: स्थितिन्यासो गृहस्थस्य सृष्ट्याख्यो ब्रह्मचारिणः। मुमुक्षोः संह्यतिन्यासः एवं न्यासस्त्रिधा मतः ।
quotations.context: Quoted on page 15 to explain the three types of nyāsa (sthiti, sṛṣṭi, saṃhāra) and which type of worshipper should perform them.

footnotes_endnotes.content: (This text has been printed with the commentary of Alasiṅga-bhaṭṭa by Sampurnananda Sanskrit University, Vāraṇāsi, 1982. The above excerpt is from the sixth chapter of the text; the topical divisions of the text is mine)

alternative_viewpoints: Different texts emphasize different aspects of worship. For example, on page 17, it is noted that 'Some texts (like jayākhya-saṃhitā) attach great importance to [mānasa-yāga] while some other texts (like Pādma-saṃhitā) do not at all mention it.'

There are different types of nyāsa suitable for different categories of worshippers. On page 15, it explains that sthiti-nyāsa is for householders, sṛṣṭi-nyāsa is for celibates, and saṃhāra-nyāsa is for those desiring emancipation.
On page 35, different mantras are prescribed for japa based on the worshipper's goal: the eight-syllabled mantra for emancipation and the twelve-syllabled mantra for prosperity.
